title: Women scholars today
hookLine: women teaching fiqh, hadith and Qur'an across the world

lines: THE MEN GET ALL YOUR TIME.
cards: A group of women in Medina has a complaint, and they bring it straight to the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him. The men, they say, are always around you. They get all your time.
So give us a day of our own. The report is in Sahih al-Bukhari. He agrees.
He promises them a day, meets them on it, and teaches them. No one in the report tells them to wait for their husbands to pass the lessons on. They asked for a teacher, and they got one.

teach.h: MEN AND WOMEN, SIDE BY SIDE.
teach.b: Begin with the Qur'an, which speaks to women and men side by side.

In Pickthall's translation, one verse runs: "Lo! men who surrender unto Allah, and women who surrender, and men who believe and women who believe," and it goes on, pair after pair, the truthful, the patient, the humble, the fasting, the ones who remember Allah, and promises all of them forgiveness and a reward.
Then the women who asked for a day. They didn't wait for knowledge to trickle down to them.
Tradition says the companions brought their questions to a woman too: 'Aisha, the Prophet's wife.
Al-Bukhari's collection carries her reports, and in some she corrects what others had passed on, as when she answers a report about the dead and the weeping of their families.

teach.h: WOMEN IN THE CHAINS, THEN AND NOW.
teach.b: Tradition remembers women after her too, who taught hadith and law in their own cities, and whose names stand in the chains of transmission alongside men's.
One of them, Karima of Merv, is remembered for teaching Sahih al-Bukhari itself. And today?
Women teach the Qur'an and its recitation, hadith, and fiqh, the law of daily life, in mosques, seminaries and colleges, in living rooms and online classes.
Communities and schools of thought hold different views on how and where women should teach, and to whom, and those views are held seriously.
But the line from the hook still runs: women asking for a teacher, and a Prophet who set the day.

how: Muslim women study and teach Qur'an recitation, hadith and fiqh in mosques, seminaries, universities and online, and communities differ on the settings in which women teach.

o: women who study Islam only to teach their own children
female students allowed to sit in on classes taught by men
women who teach Qur'an, hadith and law, in a line back to 'Aisha

p: asked the Prophet for a day

s: in the report, the women were told to learn from their husbands
the Prophet promised them a day of their own, met them, and taught them.
the Qur'an addresses believing men and women side by side
"men who surrender unto Allah, and women who surrender" (33:35, Pickthall), pair after pair.
in some of her reports, 'Aisha corrects what others had passed on
al-Bukhari's collection keeps reports in which she sets the record straight.

games.q: you're one of the women of Medina. the men are always around the Prophet, and you hardly get to ask anything. what do you do?
o: wait for the men to pass on what they hear.
go to the Prophet and ask for a day of your own.
games.why: they went straight to him and asked for a day. he agreed, met them, and taught them.

practice: Bring to mind a woman who taught you something that stuck, a mother, a grandmother, a teacher, an aunt in a kitchen, a neighbor who knew things, and picture her face as she explained it. What did she know that you didn't?
Thank her in your head for a moment, and if you pray, remember her in your prayers.

wordCard.voice: Women scholars today. Women teaching Qur'an, hadith and the law of daily life, in a line that runs back to 'Aisha and the women who asked for a day. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: a woman of knowledge, a woman scholar.

carryVoice: Your line: she teaches. And she has, from Medina all the way until now. Until tomorrow.
